clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant form of primary aldosteronism caused by germline mutations in KCNJ5, which encodes the GIRK4 potassium channel of the adrenal zona glomerulosa
Typically presents in childhood with severe, often treatment-resistant hypertension and hypokalaemia

Distinct from glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism (familial hyperaldosteronism type 1); it is generally not corrected by dexamethasone and dexamethasone may paradoxically worsen aldosterone secretion in some patients
The phenotype is variable, from florid disease with massive bilateral adrenal hyperplasia needing bilateral adrenalectomy to milder disease responsive to mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism
Biochemistry shows elevated aldosterone with suppressed renin, and the hybrid steroids 18-hydroxycortisol and 18-oxocortisol are typically raised
The mutations impair channel selectivity, causing sodium influx, membrane depolarisation, calcium entry and autonomous aldosterone production
Germline genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and informs cascade family screening
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hyperaldosteronism type 3 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline mutations in KCNJ5, which encodes the G-protein-activated inwardly rectifying potassium channel GIRK4 in the adrenal zona glomerulosa. Mutations near the channel selectivity filter cause loss of potassium selectivity and pathological sodium conductance, depolarising the cell, opening voltage-gated calcium channels and raising intracellular calcium. This drives constitutive transcription of aldosterone synthase and autonomous aldosterone hypersecretion independent of the renin-angiotensin system, with resulting sodium retention, potassium wasting and hypertension. The same channel is somatically mutated in many sporadic aldosterone-producing adenomas.
additionalDifferentials: Other familial hyperaldosteronism subtypes (type 1 glucocorticoid-remediable, type 2, type 4 with CACNA1H)
Apparent mineralocorticoid excess or Liddle syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio as the screening test, showing high aldosterone with suppressed renin
Confirmatory aldosterone suppression testing where the diagnosis is unclear
Serum potassium and acid-base assessment for hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Urinary or plasma hybrid steroids 18-hydroxycortisol and 18-oxocortisol
Adrenal CT and, in selected cases, adrenal venous sampling to assess lateralisation
KCNJ5 germline genetic testing with cascade family screening
redFlags: Severe childhood-onset hypertension resistant to multiple agents
Profound or symptomatic hypokalaemia causing arrhythmia or weakness
Massive bilateral adrenal enlargement that may require bilateral adrenalectomy
Target-organ damage such as left ventricular hypertrophy or stroke from early sustained hypertension
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on severity: milder cases are controlled with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, whereas florid disease with bilateral hyperplasia may need bilateral adrenalectomy and lifelong steroid replacement; early diagnosis and blood-pressure control limit cardiovascular and renal damage.
pitfalls: Assuming, as in type 1 disease, that dexamethasone will control aldosterone, when it usually does not and can worsen it in this subtype
Attributing resistant paediatric hypertension to essential hypertension and missing a monogenic cause
Failing to exclude secondary causes of hypokalaemia before genetic testing
Overlooking family screening once a KCNJ5 mutation is identified
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Primary Aldosteronism
management: Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists such as spironolactone or eplerenone as first-line medical therapy to block the aldosterone excess
Correction of hypokalaemia and control of hypertension with additional antihypertensive agents as needed
Bilateral adrenalectomy with subsequent lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement for florid, treatment-resistant disease with massive hyperplasia
Avoid dexamethasone, which does not correct and may paradoxically worsen aldosterone secretion in this type
Monitoring of blood pressure, serum potassium and cardiovascular and renal end-organ damage
Genetic counselling with KCNJ5 testing and cascade family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
